hypotheses.hypothesis: Partial substitution of heavy Hf with a lighter refractory element (e.g., replacing 50% of Hf with Ti) will reduce the overall density while retaining a single-phase BCC solid solution and preserving high yield strength at both room temperature and ~1000 °C.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr, a refractory high‐entropy alloy with a single disordered BCC phase and density ≈10.21 g/cm³.
hypotheses.intervention: Replace approximately 50 atomic % of Hf with Ti, forming an alloy composition such as (Hf0.5Ti0.5)MoTaTiZr.
hypotheses.conditions: As‐cast condition; mechanical testing performed at room temperature and at elevated temperature around 1000 °C under compression at a strain rate of ~10⁻³ s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Maintained BCC solid solution with lattice distortion; similar atomic radii of Hf and Ti ensure high entropy stabilization.
hypotheses.mechanism: Ti has a much lower atomic mass (and density) than Hf while its similar size allows it to substitute into the existing lattice without major disruption. The high-entropy effect and resultant lattice distortion that underpins the solution strengthening mechanism (as discussed in the paper and supported by references such as PMC7514121::web::017::4_2_solution_hardening_mechanism) are preserved, ensuring that the strength is not sacrificed despite a lower overall density.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Reduction in density (direction: lower density, roughly estimated reduction on the order of 10–20% if Hf is partially replaced) while maintaining comparable yield strength at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
hypotheses.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with high yield strength and density of 10.21 g/cm³.
hypotheses.boundary: The alloy must remain single-phase BCC from room temperature to ~1000 °C and the substitution fraction should not exceed the limit where lattice mismatch would trigger secondary phase formation.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact quantitative impacts on yield strength and ductility require experimental calibration; the substitution level must be optimized to balance density reduction against possible changes in lattice distortion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare the modified alloy (Hf0.5Ti0.5)MoTaTiZr by vacuum arc melting under similar conditions as the base alloy. Perform X-ray diffraction (XRD) to verify the BCC single-phase structure and conduct compression tests at room temperature and ~1000 °C.
measurements: Compression yield strength and ultimate strength at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy shows either a significant drop (e.g., >20% lower strength) at room or elevated temperatures compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr or exhibits formation of secondary phases, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the understanding from the paper that refractory elements can be substituted while retaining a single BCC phase and achieving high-temperature strength, and on the noted effect that Ti addition helps reduce density (PMC7514121::web::020::5_conclusions).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a systematic partial replacement of the heavy Hf with Ti in the as-cast material to lower density while leveraging Ti’s contribution to solid solution strengthening—a pathway not explored in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Partial substitution of the heavy element Ta with a lighter element Nb will decrease the alloy density while potentially enhancing ductility and preserving high-temperature strength.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr featuring a single disordered BCC phase with density ~10.21 g/cm³ and high strength at both room and elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.intervention: Replace around 50 atomic % of Ta with Nb, yielding a composition such as HfMo(Nb0.5Ta0.5)TiZr.
hypotheses.conditions: Retain as-cast processing via vacuum arc melting; perform mechanical compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C at a strain rate of ~10⁻³ s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A homogeneous BCC solid solution with lattice distortion contributed by multi-element mixing; Nb’s atomic size and modulus differences relative to Ta create comparable solid solution strengthening.
hypotheses.mechanism: Ta (atomic weight ~181 g/mol) is significantly heavier than Nb (~93 g/mol). Exchanging part of Ta for Nb will lower the overall density of the alloy. In addition, previous results in refractory HEAs (as seen in the paper’s subtraction study) indicated that the presence of Nb can improve ductility and help maintain elevated temperature strength. The mechanism is driven by modified solid solution strengthening and the beneficial effect of Nb on high-temperature performance (as discussed in PMC7514121::web::009::3_results and conclusions).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A reduced density (direction: lower density, potentially on the order of 10–15% reduction in the Ta contributing fraction) while maintaining or modestly enhancing ductility and keeping yield strength comparable at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
hypotheses.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with high strength and ductility characteristics and density of ~10.21 g/cm³.
hypotheses.boundary: The modified alloy must not form secondary phases on partial substitution, and its microstructure must remain a single-phase BCC from room temperature through 1000 °C; the substitution ratio must be low enough to avoid deterioration of high-temperature strength.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Precise mechanical property retention and the degree of density reduction are subject to experimental validation; there is uncertainty regarding the optimum substitution fraction to fully maintain high yield strengths while reducing density.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the alloy HfMo(Nb0.5Ta0.5)TiZr using the same vacuum arc melting and re-melting protocol. Characterize phase stability via XRD and perform compression tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C.
measurements: Compression test for yield strength and ductility at room and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the resultant alloy exhibits a significant decrease in yield strength (>20% reduction) or shows secondary phases that indicate loss of a stable BCC single-phase, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that elemental subtraction (such as Nb vs. Ta variations) affects ductility and high-temperature strength, and the known solid solution strengthening effects from Nb substitution (PMC7514121::web::007::3_results).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically targets the heavy Ta element for partial substitution with Nb to reduce density while potentially enhancing room temperature ductility—a method not executed in the paper’s reported compositions.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Minor addition of aluminum (Al) to replace a fraction of Hf (i.e., a substitution of a heavy element with a light one) will lower the alloy density and introduce a secondary strengthening mechanism via potential nanoscale precipitates, all while maintaining the high-temperature BCC solid solution.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr with a disordered BCC structure and high performance at room and elevated temperatures, but with relatively high density.
hypotheses.intervention: Substitute approximately 5 atomic % of Hf with Al, resulting in a composition such as (Hf0.95Al0.05)MoTaTiZr.
hypotheses.conditions: Maintain as-cast processing; establish that the alloy retains a single BCC phase and test compressive mechanical properties at room temperature and around 1000 °C, with a strain rate near 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Retention of a high-entropy BCC solid solution with additional minor Al atoms either in solid solution or forming coherent, nano-precipitates that hinder dislocation motion.
hypotheses.mechanism: Al has a very low atomic mass and density relative to Hf, so its incorporation is expected to lower the overall density. In addition, based on principles from NiAl-based systems (TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::003) and using concepts similar to precipitation hardening in superalloys, the presence of a small fraction of Al may create finely dispersed obstacles (if precipitates form) or enhance lattice distortion, thereby maintaining or even slightly enhancing the alloy’s strength at both room and elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A modest reduction in density (direction: lower overall density, expected to be a few percentage points reduction) with maintained or slightly improved yield strength and ductility at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
hypotheses.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with density ~10.21 g/cm³ and excellent strength at room and elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: The Al addition must be kept low (around 5 at.%) to avoid triggering intermetallic phase formation or ordering that would compromise the single-phase BCC structure. The beneficial effects are expected only if the high-entropy stabilization is preserved.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While Al addition is promising for density reduction, the exact impact on mechanical properties is less established in these refractory HEAs, making the quantitative performance changes less predictable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare (Hf0.95Al0.05)MoTaTiZr via vacuum arc melting under identical conditions as the parent alloy, then verify the phase stability by XRD and measure density, as well as perform compression tests at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
measurements: Compression test (yield strength, ductility) at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy exhibits formation of secondary phases, a significant drop (>20%) in yield strength at room temperature or at 1000 °C, or if density is not reduced relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the mechanisms behind density reduction and solid solution strengthening in superalloy systems (TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::003, TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::008) along with the high-entropy alloy principles discussed in the paper (PMC7514121::web::020::5_conclusions).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a light element (Al) into the refractory HEA composition as a single intervention aimed at lowering density while potentially accessing a dual mechanism of solid solution and nano-precipitation strengthening—a strategy not explored in the paper.

paper_did: Fabricated equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys and five derivative alloys obtained by subtracting one element at a time (HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi) via vacuum arc melting with multiple re-melts to improve chemical homogeneity.
Characterized the microstructure using SEM-EDS and X-ray diffraction to confirm a single-phase, disordered BCC solid solution with a dendritic structure.
Conducted compression tests on cylindrical samples at room temperature and elevated temperatures (800 °C, 1000 °C, 1200 °C, and 1400 °C) under a strain rate of ~10⁻³ s⁻¹.
Calculated and discussed the solid solution strengthening mechanism, including lattice distortion effects and comparisons of experimental shear moduli to rule-of-mixtures predictions.
paper_reported: All studied alloys stabilized as a single disordered BCC phase and exhibited a dendritic microstructure with element partitioning (e.g., Ta and Mo enrichment in dendrites).

Mechanical performance varied with composition: Addition of Mo significantly increased room-temperature yield strength (with some sacrifice in ductility), Nb enhanced ductility and high-temperature performance, while Ti and Zr modified strength and toughness in opposite ways.
HfMoNbTaTi showed the best overall performance with 27% compressive strain at room temperature and a promising yield strength at elevated temperatures (e.g., 367 MPa at 1400 °C).

The dominant strengthening mechanism was identified as solid solution strengthening attributable to severe lattice distortion, with experimental shear moduli approximately 30% lower than predicted by simple mixing rules.
paper_proposed: Future composition modifications—including further tuning of elemental ratios—to balance strength, ductility, density, and high‐temperature properties.
The application of anti-oxidation coatings for improved high-temperature performance in air.
Further research into the origin of the reduced shear modulus and testing whether the observed elemental effects extend to other refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) systems.

testable.reason: The hypothesis provides a clear experimental route by synthesizing (Hf0.5Ti0.5)MoTaTiZr and comparing its density, phase (via XRD), and compression properties at room temperature and ~1000 °C against the baseline alloy.

beyond_paper.reason: It proposes a novel partial substitution of Hf with Ti rather than a complete elemental removal, thereby addressing density reduction in a way not explored by the paper’s subtraction method.

critique.evidence_quote: ‘With Ti or Zr addition, the elevated‐temperature strength and the density decreases.’ (PMC7514121::web::020::5_conclusions)
critique.fix: Reduce the substitution fraction of Hf with Ti (e.g., lower than 50%) or co-add another high-melting element to help preserve high-temperature strength while still reducing density.

sound.reason: Partial replacement of heavy Ta with Nb is consistent with the paper’s observations that Nb improves ductility and contributes to high-temperature strength, while Ta increases strength but reduces toughness.

testable.reason: The hypothesis sets a clear intervention—replacing ~50% of Ta with Nb in HfMoTaTiZr to form HfMo(Nb0.5Ta0.5)TiZr—and outlines appropriate comparisons using density, XRD for phase purity, and compression testing at defined temperatures.

beyond_paper.reason: It goes beyond the paper by proposing a partial substitution strategy rather than outright removal of Ta, thus combining benefits of both elements in a new stoichiometry.

critique.evidence_quote: ‘One should add more Nb for higher ductility.’ (PMC7514121::web::020::5_conclusions)
critique.fix: No major fix required; however, ensure the substitution level is optimized to maintain the desired single-phase BCC structure and high-temperature strength.

sound.reason: Introducing a 5 at.% addition of Al to replace part of Hf risks destabilizing the single-phase BCC structure due to differences in atomic size and mixing enthalpy, and the mechanism invoking nanoscale precipitate strengthening is not supported by the paper’s high-entropy design criteria.

testable.reason: The experimental design does not include a heat-treatment or advanced characterization (e.g., TEM) to confirm the formation and role of nanoscale precipitates, making it hard to distinguish this mechanism from simple solid solution effects.

beyond_paper.reason: The idea of using lightweight Al to reduce density and induce precipitate strengthening is a standard textbook approach in superalloys and is not specifically motivated by, or derived from, the findings of this paper.

critique.evidence_quote: ‘All the alloys at the as‐cast state form a single BCC disorder solid solution phase…’ (PMC7514121::web::008::3_results)
critique.fix: Incorporate a controlled post-casting heat treatment designed to promote coherent nano-precipitate formation, and include transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis to conclusively verify the precipitate structure while ensuring the BCC matrix is maintained.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Partial substitution of a fraction of Hf with aluminum (Al) in HfMoTaTiZr will reduce the alloy’s density while retaining or even enhancing its high‐temperature strengthening via controlled precipitation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with a single-phase BCC (or similar disordered solid solution) structure, a density of 10.21 g/cm³, and high yield strength maintained from room temperature to near 1000 °C.
hypotheses.intervention: Replace approximately 20 atomic percent of the Hf content with Al (i.e. form an alloy with a modified ratio Hf(0.8)Al(0.2)MoTaTiZr), keeping the other components unchanged.
hypotheses.conditions: The alloy is produced by conventional arc-melting and suction casting; post‐processing (if needed) to obtain a homogeneous BCC structure should be performed. Mechanical tests will be conducted at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C under compressive loading.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a homogeneous solid-solution BCC matrix with finely dispersed Al-enriched nano-precipitates (possibly sigma or other intermetallic phases) that result from the lattice mismatch induced by Al addition.
hypotheses.mechanism: Aluminum has a very low atomic mass compared to Hf, so partial substitution reduces the overall density. In addition, the smaller atomic size of Al compared to Hf introduces additional lattice distortion that can enhance solid solution strengthening. The presence of controlled, homogeneously distributed fine precipitates (similar to the sigma phase formation observed in Al0.8NbTiV alloys [PMC8074761::web::004]), further impedes dislocation motion at both room and high temperatures.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The density should decrease (targeting a reduction of roughly 10–20% in specific density) while the yield strength remains at least at 90–100% of the original values at room temperature and near 1000 °C. The specific yield strength (strength/density) is expected to improve.
hypotheses.baseline: Original as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with density of 10.21 g/cm³ and known high mechanical performance at RT and elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: The intervention is valid if the alloy retains its microstructural phase stability and mechanical integrity (yield strength and ductility) in the temperature range from ambient to approximately 1000 °C under compressive loading.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact nature and stability of the Al-driven precipitates at ~1000 °C is not well established and may depend critically on the precise composition and thermal history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys – the original HfMoTaTiZr and the modified Hf(0.8)Al(0.2)MoTaTiZr – by identical casting and heat-treatment procedures. Characterize the microstructures by XRD and SEM/EDS to confirm phase stability and precipitate dispersion. Perform compressive tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C to determine yield strength and ductility, and measure the densities using hydrostatic weighing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy exhibits less than a 5% reduction in density relative to the original or if its yield strength reduces below 90% of the original values at any test temperature, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies a similar precipitation hardening approach—via partial elemental substitution with a lightweight element (Al)—to a heavy refractory alloy (HfMoTaTiZr), aiming to reduce density while maintaining strength up to ~1000 °C, a regime not explored in the referenced work.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Ta with vanadium (V) in HfMoTaTiZr will lower the alloy’s density while preserving its high-temperature mechanical properties by retaining a stable disordered BCC phase enhanced by solid solution and precipitation strengthening.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a high density (10.21 g/cm³) and a uniform, single-phase solid solution (likely BCC) that exhibits excellent strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.intervention: Replace roughly 20 atomic percent of Ta with V (e.g., modify the alloy composition to HfMo[Ta0.8V0.2]TiZr) while keeping the concentrations of Hf, Mo, Ti, and Zr unchanged.
hypotheses.conditions: Standard vacuum-arc melting and casting processes, with subsequent homogenization and heat treatments designed to stabilize the desired phase. Mechanical testing from room temperature up to around 1000 °C under controlled compressive loading.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A retained BCC solid-solution structure that incorporates V uniformly. The altered local chemistry is expected to promote subtle lattice distortions and possibly lead to the formation of well-dispersed, V-influenced intermetallic precipitates that contribute to strengthening.
hypotheses.mechanism: Ta is one of the heaviest constituents in the alloy; substituting part of it with V (which is significantly lighter) will reduce the overall alloy density. Vanadium, when incorporated into the BCC lattice, can contribute to solid solution strengthening similarly to its role in other refractory systems. The slight change in mixing enthalpy may also lead to the controlled formation of precipitates beneficial at high temperatures, thus maintaining yield strength even near 1000 °C.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The revised alloy is anticipated to have a modestly lower density (targeting a ~10–15% reduction in mass fraction contributed by Ta) and retain a yield strength comparable to the original alloy at both room temperature and near 1000 °C.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy’s density of 10.21 g/cm³ and its high strength performance as originally measured.
hypotheses.boundary: The intervention must maintain a stable BCC (or equivalent high-temperature) phase without the formation of coarse, deleterious intermetallics, and ensure mechanical performance is not degraded over the temperature range RT to ~1000 °C.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While V is known as a beneficial lightweight alloying addition in refractory alloys, the exact influence on precipitate formation and high-temperature stability in a five-component system like HfMoTaTiZr is not fully predictable.

hypotheses.builds_on: The principle demonstrated in PMC8074761 where modifying the composition by lightening the constituent elements stimulated solid solution and precipitation strengthening, while also lowering density.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This approach targets the replacement of a heavy refractory element (Ta) with a much lighter element (V) within a high-entropy refractory system and examines the impact on high-temperature strength up to ~1000 °C—a temperature range beyond what was studied in the referenced paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The addition of a minor amount of scandium (Sc) to HfMoTaTiZr will reduce the overall density and refine the microstructure through grain refinement and nano-scale precipitate formation, thereby retaining high yield strength at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy exhibiting a high density (10.21 g/cm³) with a coarse-to-moderate grain structure and a stable high-temperature phase.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a small doping level (e.g., 2–5 at.%) of Sc into the HfMoTaTiZr alloy without altering the primary refractory alloying ratio substantially.
hypotheses.conditions: Standard casting and homogenization heat treatments ensuring complete dissolution of Sc followed by a controlled cooling process to encourage fine grain formation. Testing should cover room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1000 °C under mechanical loading conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain refinement and the formation of coherent, nanoscale Sc-rich precipitates embedded within the BCC matrix that act as barriers to dislocation motion.
hypotheses.mechanism: Scandium has a very low atomic mass and a high melting point, making it a promising microalloying addition in high-temperature alloys (similar in spirit to its role in some aluminum alloys). Its addition is expected to enhance nucleation rates during solidification and inhibit grain growth, resulting in a refined microstructure. Moreover, nanoscale Sc-rich precipitates can provide additional precipitation hardening without detracting significantly from the alloy’s high-temperature stability, effectively maintaining yield strength while lowering density slightly.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A modest reduction in density (on the order of 3–5%) along with a refined grain structure that ensures maintained or even slightly improved yield strength at room temperature and near 1000 °C, compared to the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with its original grain size, density, and high-temperature strength characteristics.
hypotheses.boundary: The benefits must persist under isothermal mechanical testing from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C; the microalloying must not trigger adverse phase transformations or coarsening of precipitates at elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While Sc is effective in aluminum systems, its behavior and the stability of Sc-rich precipitates in a multi-component refractory high-entropy alloy are less well documented, especially under prolonged exposure to 1000 °C.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloys: one with the original HfMoTaTiZr composition and one with an additional 3 at.% Sc. Conduct microstructural characterizations (grain size analysis via SEM/TEM, XRD for phase identification) and measure densities. Characterized the alloys using X‐ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to establish phase formation (a BCC matrix in the as-cast state and the formation of sigma precipitates after heat treatment) and measured mechanical properties (compressive strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 800 °C) as well as density
paper_reported: All as‐cast AlxNbTiV alloys show a single BCC solid-solution phase with lattice parameter reduction and yield strength improvement as the Al content increases; specifically, the Al0.8NbTiV alloy was identified as optimal for its well‐balanced mechanical properties and low density.

Minor additions of Co or Ni to Al0.8NbTiV further enhanced the room-temperature yield strength by solid-solution strengthening, and after heat treatment at 1100 °C, the alloys developed homogeneously distributed sigma precipitates (with distinct Nb-rich and Co/Ni-rich variants) within the BCC matrix that act as significant strengthening agents.

The presence and uniform distribution of the sigma phase lead to superior specific yield strengths at elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) compared to other single-phase RHEAs and conventional Ni-based superalloys (e.g., Inconel 718).

hypotheses.structural_mediator: Single-phase BCC structure retention with modified lattice parameters due to Nb substitution.
hypotheses.mechanism: Nb has a considerably lower density than Hf while still being a refractory element. The similar atomic radii and compatibility in forming a BCC solid solution help maintain the dislocation-based deformation mechanism. hypotheses.boundary: Applicability is expected for tensile tests from room temperature up to ~1000 °C under strain rates similar to those used in prior high-temperature tensile tests.

Characterized the as‐printed material’s microstructure using SEM, EBSD, EDS, and X‐ray micro-CT to reveal both single-phase (fcc austenite) and dual-phase (fcc austenite + bcc ferrite) regions, including cellular substructures (~5 µm) and elemental segregation (Si, Mo, S, Cr, Ni enrichment along substructure boundaries).

Performed in situ micro-compression tests on FIB-milled micro-pillars (4 µm × 4 µm × 8 µm) along the [001] orientation to record stress–strain behavior, deformation twinning, and differences in mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and Young’s modulus) between single-phase and dual-phase regions.
paper_reported: Dual-phase structures, which include chemical segregation and additional phase boundaries, exhibited a slightly lower yield strength (~418 MPa) but a significantly higher Young’s modulus (~38 GPa) compared with the single-phase regions (~428 MPa and ~21 GPa, respectively).

Deformation twinning was identified as the dominating mechanism during compression, with distinct twin spacings in single-phase (~44 nm) versus dual-phase (~395 nm) pillars and clear load drops in the stress–strain curves correlating with twin formation.

Chemical mapping confirmed that unwanted elemental segregation (enrichment of Si, Mo, S, Cr, and Ni with Fe depletion) occurs along the cellular substructure boundaries, which is implicated in the mechanical performance variations.
